ta-l1d33q1-d1e97.summary: A divisio textus for Distinction 33. Having treated essence, persons, and properties, Lombard compares them: first the properties with essence and persons, then the persons with the essence (Dist. 34). He shows that the properties are in the persons, that they are the persons, and that they are the divine essence, arguing by reason and authority from divine simplicity, which allows neither that what is in God differs from him nor that the haver differs from what is had. He then excludes the contrary error, setting out its rational arguments (if the properties are the persons they do not determine them; the uniting cannot be the distinguishing; properties in the essence would determine it), answering some and declining others as too difficult, and its arguments from authority. Five articles are announced: whether the properties are the divine essence; whether they are the persons; whether they are in the persons and in the essence; whether essential and personal adjectives can be predicated of the properties; and whether contrary opinions about the notions can be held without sin.
claims: By divine simplicity the properties are in the persons, are the persons, and are the essence.

ta-l1d33q1-d1e147.summary: First argument that the relations are not the divine essence. Divine relatives are relative by being, not only by being said, or Sabellianism follows (Dist. 31), and the being of such relatives is to be toward another (the Philosopher), while the essence's being is absolute.
claims: Relatives by being have being toward another.

ta-l1d33q1-d1e150.summary: Second argument. Things really the same are in whatever either is in, but the essence is in the Son and paternity is not, so they are not the same.
claims: What is really identical shares location.

ta-l1d33q1-d1e153.summary: Third argument, against 'same in reality, different in concept'. Either that concept is something real or not. If not, since distinction is only by relations, the persons would be only conceptually distinct; if so, whatever is real in God is had by God, and in God haver and had are the same, so the essence would be the concept of paternity, and they would be the same in concept too.
claims: A merely conceptual difference makes the persons conceptually distinct.

ta-l1d33q1-d1e157.summary: Fourth argument. If property adds only a concept to the essence, so do relations said from time, which are only assisting, not inhering, otherwise God would change; so the distinguishing relations would be assisting too, not the essence.
claims: Properties would be like temporal relations.

ta-l1d33q1-d1e160.summary: Fifth argument. As the concepts of paternity and essence differ, so do those of essence and goodness, so if Augustine says God is Father by one thing and God by another for this reason, he should say God is God by one thing and good by another, which he denies; so he means a real distinction.
claims: Augustine's 'alio pater, alio Deus' would apply to goodness too.

ta-l1d33q1-d1e163.summary: Sed contra. Only God is adored with latria, and the properties are adored, as the Preface sings ('that in the persons property, in the essence unity, and in majesty equality be adored'). The paragraph then argues (as transcribed, the transition to this step is abrupt) that the properties are either something real or nothing: if nothing, the persons are not really distinct, Sabellius's heresy; if something other than the essence, there is composition in the person, and no composite is God (Dist. 8), so the persons would not be God, exceeding even Arius's error. So the properties are the divine essence.
claims: The properties are adored and so are God.
If properties were other than the essence, the persons would be composite and not God.

ta-l1d33q1-d1e169.summary: Thomas's determination. It must simply be confessed that the properties are the divine essence. The error in the text is said to be the Porretan's, who retracted it at the Council of Reims. In relation there is the respect by which it is referred to another, in which its concept consists, and its being, which it has as founded in something, quantity, essence, or the like (Dist. 8). He considered the divine relations by their respect, by which they imply nothing inhering, since some relations posit nothing real, and so called them assisting or externally attached. Properly, relations that are assisting have no foundation in the thing and come only from another's relation to it, as right in a column, and such are God's relations to creatures. But the relations distinguishing the persons are founded on something truly real, the communication of nature, and so are real relations with being founded in the nature of the thing. By divine simplicity there can be only one being in God, and being, what is, and that by which differ not, so the being of paternity can be no other than the being of the essence, and since the being of the essence is the essence and the being of paternity is paternity, paternity is really the essence and makes no composition with it. Since a true respect pertaining to the nature remains, reason can distinguish the relations, which do not pertain to the concept of essence, by that respect, though the essence is not distinguished, since that opposed and distinction-causing respect is not in its concept. So properties and essence are the same in reality and differ in concept. In creatures the being of a real relation differs from the being of the substance related, so relations inhere and compose with the subject, which does not hold in God.
claims: The properties are really the divine essence and differ only in concept.
The Porretan view of assisting relations fails because the divine relations are founded on the communication of nature.
By simplicity the being of paternity is the being of the essence.

ta-l1d33q1-d1e172.summary: Reply to the first argument. These relations are relative by being, not only by being said. 'Being' is said three ways: the quiddity or nature, as a definition signifies what it is to be; the act of essence, as living is the being of the living, first act of the soul; and the truth of composition, the copula, completed in the intellect but founded on the act of essence (Dist. 19). 'Relatives are those whose being is to be toward another' concerns being as quiddity, since a relation's nature is to be referred to another, not being as act of essence, which a relation has from its causes in a subject, referred to the subject, as every accident. So the essence's being need not be toward another, since paternity and essence are united in being as act of essence, not in being as quiddity, the concept of paternity differing from that of essence.
claims: Esse means quiddity, act of essence, or truth of composition.
Paternity and essence are one in esse as act of essence, different in esse as quiddity.

ta-l1d33q1-d1e178.summary: Reply to the second argument. Things the same are in whatever either is in as to that in which they are the same. Paternity and essence are the same in being, so as the essence's being is in the Son, so is paternity's being, since there is only one being in God. But paternity has something in which it is not one with the essence, its concept, by which its respect can be in the Father and not in the Son, distinguishing Father from Son, so the argument commits the fallacy of accident. No creaturely likeness should be sought, since nothing created resembles divine simplicity, where the haver is that by which it has; likenesses from points or differences in a genus mislead more than help (Boethius: in immaterial things one should not be led by imagination).
claims: Paternity and essence share being but not concept; the argument commits the fallacy of accident.
Creaturely analogies to divine simplicity mislead.

ta-l1d33q1-d1e182.summary: Reply to the third argument. The reply is good. 'Ratio' means either what is in the reasoner (the act or power of reason) or an intention, signifying a definition or an argument. 'Different concepts of paternity and essence' takes ratio as an intention signifying definition: though there is no definition, genus, difference, or composition in God, if something were defined there, paternity and essence would have different definitions. Intentions are not in things but in the soul, yet have something corresponding in reality, the nature to which the intellect attributes them, as the intention of genus is not in an ass but the nature of animal is. So the different concepts in God are not in reality, but something corresponds to them, the truth of the thing to which the intention is attributed. So it does not follow that God is those concepts, only that he has them: haver and had are the same in God for what is had as things, not as intentions, as God has a name but is not a name; he is goodness and paternity because he has them, but not 'relation', though he has a relation.
claims: The concepts distinguishing paternity and essence are intentions with a real foundation.
In God haver and had are identical for things, not for intentions.

ta-l1d33q1-d1e185.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. The concepts of relations said of God from time have no being in the divine reality on which to be founded, as the personal relations do, so the cases differ.
claims: Temporal relations have no foundation in God; personal relations do.

ta-l1d33q1-d1e188.summary: Reply to the fifth argument. Knowledge is divided against substance only by its genus, quality ('no quality is substance' is immediate, 'no knowledge is substance' mediate), and so in all genera. In God only the common character of relation remains among the categories (Dist. 8), so the relative in God has a concept and mode of predication divided against substance, while knowledge, goodness, and the like have no common generic character divided against substance; substance takes the place of quality or quantity. So their concepts differ from substance's as species from genus, not as opposed, and as in creatures one is qualified and knowing by the same, in God one is substance and knowing by the same, but not substance and Father, since relation, divided against substance, keeps its generic character and mode of signifying in God.
claims: Attributes differ from essence as species from genus; relations differ as opposed genus.
So God is good by what he is God, but not Father by what he is God.

ta-l1d33q1-d1e200.summary: First argument that the properties are not the persons. Things really the same multiply together, so there would be as many persons as properties, which are five.
claims: Five properties would be five persons.

ta-l1d33q1-d1e203.summary: Second argument. God is called triune for the trinity of persons, so if the notions are persons he would be 'quinune' for five notions, the Father triune and the Son 'binune'.
claims: Notions would multiply 'trinus'.

ta-l1d33q1-d1e206.summary: Third argument. Augustine says everything said relatively is something besides its relation, as a coin is something besides being a price. The Father is referred to the Son, so beyond the relation there is something underlying it, the hypostasis or person.
claims: Every relative is something beyond its relation.

ta-l1d33q1-d1e210.summary: Fourth argument. Nothing distinguishes itself, and properties distinguish persons (Damascene).
claims: Properties distinguish persons.

ta-l1d33q1-d1e213.summary: Fifth argument. Every concrete adds to its abstract, as white to whiteness, and persons are signified concretely, properties abstractly.
claims: Concrete adds to abstract.

ta-l1d33q1-d1e216.summary: Sed contra. Hilary says the Son is nothing but Son, and 'Son' signifies relation, so the whole of what the Son is, his essence and hypostasis, is the relation of filiation.
claims: The Son is nothing but Son.

ta-l1d33q1-d1e219.summary: Second sed contra. Every form is principle of what it informs in some respect of its being, so if paternity were other than the Father it would be principle and prior to the Father.
claims: A distinct form would be prior to the Father.

ta-l1d33q1-d1e222.summary: Thomas's determination. There are three opinions. The Porretans said the properties are in the persons as assisting and are not the persons, which fails, since either the property is something real, and then composition follows if it is not the person, or nothing, and then there is no real distinction. Praepositinus said the properties are the persons in reality and not distinct from them even conceptually, so that in God there are only essence and persons, abstract property names standing for the concrete ('I ask your kindness'), and the persons distinguish themselves. This fails too, since one person has several relations as related to different persons, and something is attributed to the property (distinguishing) and not to the person (being distinguished), so they differ in mode of signifying, which would be empty unless there were different concepts with something real corresponding. So properties and persons are the same in reality and differ in concept, as properties and essence do, but whereas property and essence differ as concepts of different genera, property and person differ as abstract and concrete in the same genus. In creatures the concrete has composition and perfection, being signified as per se existing, and the abstract has simplicity and imperfection, being signified as form, which neither operates nor subsists in itself. Neither concept fits God wholly, so nothing is said of God properly (Liber de causis), neither abstract for imperfection nor concrete for composition, but each truly in part: the concrete for perfection, the abstract for simplicity.
claims: Properties and persons are really the same and differ as abstract and concrete in one genus.
Against Praepositinus, properties must be admitted, since properties distinguish and persons are distinguished.
Abstract names signify God's simplicity and concrete names his perfection.

ta-l1d33q1-d1e225.summary: Reply to the first argument. Properties are the same as persons in being, but persons are not distinguished by being, so the number of properties does not give the number of persons. Persons are distinguished only by relative opposition, which can yield no more than three, so opposed relations are persons and two such relations are two persons, while unopposed relations in one person are two relations or properties but one person.
claims: Only opposed relations multiply persons.

ta-l1d33q1-d1e229.summary: Reply to the second argument. Relations are signified in God as forms or qualities, and the number of forms does not posit number in things simply, only the number of supposits, as Socrates is not 'triune' for having three properties; so the Father is not triune for three notions, but God is triune for three persons or supposits.
claims: 'Trinus' follows the number of supposits.

ta-l1d33q1-d1e232.summary: Reply to the third argument. Augustine's saying holds in God and creatures differently: in creatures what is said relatively underlies the relation as subject an accident, so they are different; in God what is said relatively is the relation itself, since in God there is no real difference, only a conceptual one, between essence, the person having the essence, and the distinguishing property.
claims: In God the relative is the relation itself.

ta-l1d33q1-d1e235.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. A property is signified as form, and it belongs to form to distinguish, so properties distinguish persons by mode of signifying, which is grounded in the true concept of property, and no real diversity follows.
claims: Properties distinguish by mode of signifying.

ta-l1d33q1-d1e238.summary: Reply to the fifth argument. In God abstract and concrete differ only conceptually, so property differs from person as deity from God.
claims: Property differs from person as deity from God.

ta-l1d33q1-d1e250.summary: First argument that the properties are neither in the essence nor in the persons. Of things really the same, one cannot be in the other, since nothing is in itself except per accidens (the Philosopher).
claims: Nothing is in itself.

ta-l1d33q1-d1e253.summary: Second argument. Whatever a relation is in is related, and whatever is related in God is distinguished by relation, but the essence is not distinguished.
claims: What has a relation is related.

ta-l1d33q1-d1e256.summary: Third argument. Relations follow some motion or change, and there is none in God.
claims: Relations follow change.

ta-l1d33q1-d1e260.summary: Fourth argument. Whatever is in something is in it in some way, and none of the Philosopher's modes of being-in fits properties in persons.
claims: No mode of inesse fits.

ta-l1d33q1-d1e263.summary: Sed contra from the Preface: in the persons let property be adored.
claims: Property is in the persons.

ta-l1d33q1-d1e269.summary: Second sed contra. What is denominated by a form must have it in itself, and the persons are denominated from properties, the Father from paternity.
claims: Denomination requires inherence.

ta-l1d33q1-d1e272.summary: Thomas's determination. The properties are in the essence and in the persons, differently: in the essence by real identity, not as in a supposit; in the persons as in a supposit, but in two ways, since something is supposit either of the nature by which it is constituted, as humanity in Socrates, as the personal properties are in the persons, or of what comes after its constituted being, as whiteness in Socrates, as the non-personal properties, innascibility and common spiration, are conceptually in the persons; yet the supposit is not really different from what is in it, only conceptually, as concrete and abstract.
claims: Properties are in the essence by identity and in the persons as in supposits.
Personal properties are in persons as constituting nature; non-personal ones as consequent.

ta-l1d33q1-d1e275.summary: This answers the first argument: because properties are conceptually distinct and really the same as essence and persons, one is said to be in the other.
claims: Conceptual distinction allows being-in.

ta-l1d33q1-d1e278.summary: Reply to the second argument. Whatever a relation is in as in a supposit is related, as whatever whiteness is in as supposit is white. In the divine nature or essence the relative property is not as in a supposit but by real identity, so relation is not predicated concretely of the essence ('the essence is related') but by a predication of identity ('the essence is relation'), and the essence need not be distinguished. In creatures paternity is in Socrates as supposit, so Socrates is called father but not his humanity, though one might say humanity and paternity coincide, not by real identity as in God but in one supposit, Socrates.
claims: The essence is relation by identity, not related as supposit.

ta-l1d33q1-d1e282.summary: Reply to the third argument. Following motion belongs to relation insofar as it is not eternal, so eternal relations follow no motion, as, if the world were eternal, heavenly bodies would be equal or double without any motion, since the heavens do not change in quantity. The relations distinguishing the persons are eternal and follow no motion, but in place of motion in a way follow the communication and reception of the divine nature.
claims: Eternal relations follow communication of nature, not motion.

ta-l1d33q1-d1e285.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. According to Hilary there is no comparison of earthly to divine things, so none of the Philosopher's modes suffices to explain being-in in God, especially that of properties in the essence, since in creatures things of different genera never coincide in real identity as relation and substance do in God, by which paternity is in the essence as in what is conceptually pre-existing. The way non-personal properties are in persons resembles accidental form in a subject, and the way personal properties are in persons resembles differences in a species or a common nature in an inferior, though the unlikeness is greater than the likeness.
claims: No creaturely mode of being-in fits properties in the essence; some resemble accident in subject or difference in species.

ta-l1d33q1-d1e298.summary: First argument that essential adjectives are predicated of the properties. What is said of one of two really identical things is said of the other, otherwise affirmation and negation would be true of the same, and the properties are God.
claims: What is said of the identical is said of both.

ta-l1d33q1-d1e301.summary: Second argument. Some essential adjectives are predicated of properties ('immense', 'uncreated'), so all should be.
claims: Some essential adjectives fit properties.

ta-l1d33q1-d1e304.summary: Third argument. Personal adjectives agree more with properties than essential ones do, and some essential ones are predicated of properties, so much more all personal ones ('paternity begets', 'is unbegotten').
claims: Personal adjectives fit properties better.

ta-l1d33q1-d1e308.summary: Fourth argument. Boethius says no proposition is truer than one predicating the same of itself, and in the Father paternity and begetting are the same, so 'paternity begets' is true.
claims: Paternity and begetting are the same.

ta-l1d33q1-d1e311.summary: Sed contra. Essence is as really identical with the persons as property is, yet notional adjectives are not predicated of the essence because of its mode of signifying, which causes different supposition ('the essence is begotten' is false), so neither should 'filiation is begotten' be said.
claims: Mode of signifying blocks predication despite identity.

ta-l1d33q1-d1e314.summary: Thomas's determination. Property, person, and essence differ only conceptually and in mode of signifying, so adjectives must be distinguished. Those predicating an absolute condition of the thing, especially negatives like 'uncreated', are predicated of all three. Those expressing the mode of signifying by which the three differ are not. Among these, some include that mode in their principal signification ('common' the mode of essence, 'distinct' that of person, 'distinguishing' that of property), so swapping them ('the essence is distinct', 'the property is common') is false, not merely improper. Others imply the mode not by signifying it but by their mode of signifying, like those signifying by way of act, since acts belong to supposits, so they properly fit only persons, not property or essence, which are signified as forms; so 'paternity begets' or 'creates' is improper; likewise concretes imply the mode of persons, so 'paternity is wise', 'paternity is Father' (adjectivally), or 'paternity is unbegotten' are improper.
claims: Absolute and negative adjectives are said of essence, person, and property alike.
Adjectives signifying a mode (common, distinct, distinguishing) are false when transferred; act and concrete adjectives are improper of properties.

ta-l1d33q1-d1e317.summary: Reply to the first argument. Though really the same, they differ conceptually, so something can properly be said of one that is not properly said of the other.
claims: Conceptual difference allows different predication.

ta-l1d33q1-d1e320.summary: Reply to the second argument. Negative adjectives imply no determinate mode belonging properly to essence or person, but conditions that can follow either as to mode of signifying.
claims: Negative adjectives are mode-neutral.

ta-l1d33q1-d1e323.summary: Reply to the third argument. Personal adjectives agree with properties no more than essential ones as to mode of signifying, though more as to genus, both signifying relation, so they cannot be predicated of properties for the same reason. Essential adjectives are predicated more properly of the essence than personal ones of properties, since property is signified as a concept of the person, further from the supposit's perfection than the essence, which says the whole being of the supposit differently signified; yet personal adjectives cannot be predicated of the essence at all, because the distinction they signify is opposed to the mode of essence.
claims: Essential adjectives fit the essence better than personal adjectives fit properties; personal adjectives never fit the essence.

ta-l1d33q1-d1e327.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. 'To beget' signifies the same as paternity in reality but differs in mode of signifying, since it signifies as going out from a supposit, and paternity is not signified as supposit, so 'begets' cannot be predicated of it.
claims: 'Generare' requires a supposit as subject.

ta-l1d33q1-d1e339.summary: First argument that contrary opinions about the notions cannot be held without sin. Augustine says nowhere is error more dangerous than about the Trinity, and contrary opinions involve someone's error.
claims: Error about the Trinity is most dangerous.

ta-l1d33q1-d1e342.summary: Second argument. Of contradictories one is false, and some deny properties, some make them infinite, some five, some the essence, some not, so someone lies, and lies about divine things are gravest (Augustine).
claims: Contradictory opinions involve falsehood.

ta-l1d33q1-d1e345.summary: Third argument, against the excuse that Scripture says nothing about the notions. If Scripture means the biblical canon, it says nothing of persons either, so one could deny the persons, which is heretical; if the Fathers' sayings, they expressly mention properties.
claims: Silence of Scripture does not excuse.

ta-l1d33q1-d1e349.summary: Sed contra. Every sin is of faith or morals; this contrariety involves no sin of morals, which concerns actions, nor of faith, since no article is denied.
claims: No article of faith is denied.

ta-l1d33q1-d1e352.summary: Thomas's determination. Contrary opinions may concern what belongs to the faith or not. About what does not belong to it, and from which nothing contrary to faith follows, there is no sin except per accidens, such as presumption in asserting the doubtful too strongly, lying, or vainglory, since accidental causes are infinite. About what belongs to faith, either it is expressly contained in the articles, which all must know, and then contradiction involves sin in one party, simple error or heresy if pertinacity is added; or it is something from which something contrary to faith follows though not expressed or determined in faith, and then before examination shows the consequence, both can be held without sin, especially without pertinacity, but once the truth has been examined and the consequence seen, the judgement is the same as for what is determined in faith. So a simple person ignorant of Scripture who believed Jacob was Isaac's father, implying Scripture is false, would not sin until shown the consequence, but would be a heretic if he then persisted pertinaciously. So with the notions, about which nothing is expressly determined in faith, yet error about them leads to error about the persons and faith: if relations are only assisting, either composition in God or merely conceptual distinction follows, which is Sabellian, so the Porretan retracted on seeing the consequence. Those who deny the properties do not wholly deny them but implicitly place them in and identify them with the persons; denying them altogether would be heretical, as would pertinaciously defending assisting relations, which is why the text calls such people heretics.
claims: Opinions on the notions are not sinful before their consequences for faith are seen, but pertinacity after examination is heresy.
Holding relations to be merely assisting implies composition or Sabellianism.

ta-l1d33q1-d1e364.summary: An expositio textus laying out Lombard's arguments. (1) Properties are persons: properties distinguish persons, persons are eternally distinct, so properties are eternal, and nothing eternal is not in God, so they are in the persons, and whatever is in the persons is the persons, or there would be composition. (2) Properties are the essence: in God haver and had are the same, and God has the properties. (3) The opponents' first argument (the distinguishing is not the distinguished) Lombard answers by denying the major, since the persons distinguish themselves. (4) Their second (the same cannot unite and distinguish) he leaves unsolved as too difficult; its answer is in Article 1. (5) Their third (whatever has paternity is Father and begetting, so the essence would be Father and Son, Sabellianism) is answered by saying properties are in the essence without determining it, so concrete adjectives are not predicated of it. (6) Their fourth (same cause, same effect: properties determine the persons they are in, so would determine the essence) he does not answer; the answer is in Article 3. (7) To Augustine's 'he is not God by that by which he is Father', the negation can include the order of formal cause, 'not by paternity is he God', which is true, or leave it affirmed, 'that by which he is Father is not that by which he is God', which is false, since paternity is deity, though he is not called God from paternity, because of their different concepts.
claims: Lombard's arguments for identity and his unsolved objections are answered by the articles.
'Non eo est pater quo Deus' is true or false according to the scope of the negation.

ta-l1d33q1-Dd1e92.summary: The Prooemium of Distinction 33 divides Lombard's comparison of properties with essence and persons, arguing from divine simplicity that properties are in, and identical with, persons and essence, and excluding the Porretan error. It announces five articles on these identities, on predication of the properties, and on the culpability of contrary opinions.
claims: Properties are the persons and the essence.

ta-l1d33q1-Dd1e139.summary: Article 1 holds that the properties are really the divine essence and differ only in concept. Against the Porretan doctrine of assisting relations, the divine relations are founded on the communication of nature, and by simplicity the being of paternity is the being of the essence. They are one in being as act of essence, different in being as quiddity. The differing concepts are intentions with a real foundation, and relations, unlike other attributes, keep their generic character opposed to substance, so God is good but not Father by what he is God.
claims: The properties are really the essence, conceptually distinct.
Relation alone keeps its generic character in God.

ta-l1d33q1-Dd1e192.summary: Article 2 holds, against the Porretans and Praepositinus, that properties and persons are really the same and differ as abstract and concrete in one genus. Abstract names signify God's simplicity and concrete names his perfection, though neither fits wholly. Only opposed relations multiply persons, 'triune' follows supposits, and in God the relative is the relation itself.
claims: Properties and persons differ as abstract and concrete.

ta-l1d33q1-Dd1e242.summary: Article 3 holds that properties are in the essence by real identity and in the persons as in supposits: personal properties as constituting nature, non-personal ones as consequent. The essence 'is relation' by identity but is not 'related'. Eternal relations follow communication of nature, not motion, and no creaturely mode of being-in fits exactly.
claims: Properties are in the essence by identity and in persons as supposits.

ta-l1d33q1-Dd1e290.summary: Article 4 holds that absolute and negative adjectives are said alike of essence, person, and property. Adjectives that signify a mode (common, distinct, distinguishing) are false when transferred, and act-adjectives and concrete adjectives are improper of properties, since acts belong to supposits. So 'paternity begets' is improper.
claims: Act and concrete adjectives are not properly said of properties.

ta-l1d33q1-Dd1e331.summary: Article 5 holds that contrary opinions about the notions are not sinful before their consequences for faith are seen, but pertinacity after examination is heresy, as with any implicit denial of revealed truth. Holding relations to be merely assisting implies composition or Sabellianism, which is why the Porretan retracted.
claims: Error about the notions becomes heresy only with pertinacity after its consequences are shown.

ta-l1d33q1-Dd1e359.summary: The Expositio textus of Distinction 33 lays out Lombard's arguments that properties are persons and essence and the opponents' objections, some of which Lombard left unsolved and the articles answer. It resolves Augustine's 'not by that by which he is Father is he God' by the scope of the negation.
claims: Lombard's unsolved objections are answered by the articles.

ta-l1d33q1.summary: Quaestio 1 of Book I, Distinction 33 treats the relation of the properties to essence and persons. Article 1 holds, against the Porretan doctrine of assisting relations, that the properties are really the divine essence and differ only in concept, since their being is the essence's being. Article 2 holds that properties and persons are really the same, differing as abstract and concrete. Article 3 holds that properties are in the essence by identity and in the persons as in supposits. Article 4 sets rules for predicating adjectives of properties, act-adjectives fitting only persons. Article 5 holds that contrary opinions about the notions become heretical only with pertinacity after their consequences for faith are shown.
claims: The properties are really the essence and the persons, distinct only in concept.
Acts and concrete predicates belong properly to persons, not properties.
Error about the notions becomes heresy only with pertinacity.
